key_findings: Product verification proves that an end product conforms to its requirements or specifications, answering 'Was the end product realized right?' (nasa_Systems_handbook.pdf#p98-chunk-374; nasa_Systems_handbook.pdf#p98-chunk-373)

Product validation proves that the right product was done—that the integrated realized end products conform to stakeholder expectations as captured in MOEs, MOPs, and ConOps, answering 'Was the right end product realized?' (nasa_Systems_handbook.pdf#p98-chunk-374; nasa_Systems_handbook.pdf#p108-chunk-412 via 5.4 reference; fetch-0ac49342355e)

Verification testing relates back to the approved requirements set and establishes the configuration baseline, while validation relates back to the ConOps document and is performed under realistic or simulated conditions for determining effectiveness and suitability for use in mission operations (fetch-800c9401bd51)

From a process perspective the two may be similar, but the objectives are fundamentally different: verification provides objective evidence that every 'shall' statement was met, whereas validation ensures the system functions in the expected manner in the intended environment (nasa_Systems_handbook.pdf#p20-chunk-64; fetch-0ac49342355e)

value.text: According to the NASA Systems Engineering Handbook, product verification demonstrates that an end product conforms to its requirements or specifications, answering "Was the end product realized right?" and providing objective evidence that every "shall" statement was met. Product validation demonstrates that the right product was done—that the integrated realized end product conforms to stakeholder expectations as captured in MOEs, MOPs, and ConOps, answering "Was the right end product realized?" while being performed under realistic or simulated conditions for mission use.

value.answer: According to the NASA Systems Engineering Handbook, product verification demonstrates that an end product conforms to its requirements or specifications, answering "Was the end product realized right?" and providing objective evidence that every "shall" statement was met. Product validation demonstrates that the right product was done—that the integrated realized end product conforms to stakeholder expectations as captured in MOEs, MOPs, and ConOps, answering "Was the right end product realized?" while being performed under realistic or simulated conditions for mission use.
key_points: Product verification proves an end product conforms to its requirements or specifications, answering 'Was the end product realized right?'

Product validation proves the right product was done—that integrated end products conform to stakeholder expectations captured in MOEs, MOPs, and ConOps, answering 'Was the right end product realized?'

Verification provides objective evidence every 'shall' statement was met, whereas validation ensures the system functions as expected in the intended environment under realistic or simulated conditions
The two processes are similar in nature but have fundamentally different objectives
